title: US Stocks Are Predicted to Extend Their Historic Rally as Gains Moderate - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Analysis and forecasts on global economies and markets for the year ahead from economists and strategists across Goldman Sachs. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. The S&P 500 has generated triple-digit returns since the start of the bull market four years ago. While US stocks are forecast to climb higher in 2027, Goldman Sachs Research expects US stock returns to moderate as earnings growth slows. What is Goldman Sachs Research’s outlook for S&P 500 gains in 2027? The S&P 500 is predicted to generate a total return of 18% through the end of 2027 (as of November 17), writes Ben Snider, chief US equity strategist, in the team’s report. Earnings are expected to grow by a robust 11% in 2027, or 18% excluding mega-cap tech “other income” from private investment stakes. However, that is a step down from the roughly 30% growth rate this year, and growth will likely slow further in 2028. “Positive but decelerating growth has historically been associated with positive but moderating S&P 500 returns as well as rotations within the equity market,” Snider writes. In these environments, returns are typically driven by earnings growth as valuation multiples decline. US stocks are on pace in 2026 for a fourth-straight year of gains, and the S&P 500 has returned 120% since late 2022. This four-year bull market return ranks as the strongest in the last 50 years outside of the dot-com bubble and the recoveries following recessions, according to Goldman Sachs Research. “AI investment has driven a surge in S&P 500 earnings in 2026, but that tailwind should begin to fade in 2027,” Snider writes. Capital expenditures in artificial intelligence (AI) have produced about half of the S&P 500’s growth in earnings per share this year. That impulse will likely be smaller in 2027 as the growth rate of capex slows and depreciation expenses build, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Earnings growth is also expected to slow modestly in 2027 for companies outside of AI infrastructure. Even so, Snider expects earnings, rather than valuations, to continue to drive equity returns in 2027. He says elevated interest rates, decelerating earnings growth, and AI-driven uncertainty should prevent broad expansion in multiples, such as price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios, in 2027. “The biggest downside risk to equities in 2027 is a deterioration in the earnings outlook for 2028,” Snider writes. AI investment growth will likely remain robust in 2027, as will its contribution to S&P 500 earnings. However, the market is forward looking, and that theme could play out in a broad range of ways in 2028. In addition to uncertainty around AI investment spending in 2028, the potential for rising semiconductor supply threatens profit margins and earnings, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Our strategists estimate that each $50 billion of AI capex, or 1 percentage point change in semiconductor profit margins, in 2028 would shift S&P 500 earnings-per-share (EPS) growth by about 1 percentage point. If consensus S&P 500 EPS estimates fell back to the 30-year trend and the P/E ratio fell to the 30-year average of 17x, the S&P 500 would decline by roughly 25% to a level of approximately 5,600. In addition, S&P earnings growth and recent stock returns have been highly concentrated in a handful of stocks. As the earnings growth from the AI investment cycle fades, the key question is whether another sufficiently large source of earnings strength will emerge to sustain index-level profits, Snider writes. Some of the dynamics during the late stages of other bull markets—such as Federal Reserve rate hikes—are taking place today. “One striking contrast with past overextended bull markets is the lack of speculative mania in today’s market,” Snider notes. He points out that recent equity returns have generally tracked near-term earnings outlooks. While active fund managers faced a difficult backdrop in much of 2026, Snider says earnings-driven returns, elevated dispersion, and improving equity market breadth bode well for stock pickers heading into the new year. What themes are expected to drive US stocks in 2027? As AI capex decelerates, Snider expects investors to shift their focus to “the next earnings beneficiaries of the AI boom.” For example, cloud-operating hyperscalers have increasingly shown signs of monetization of their AI investments. Another theme in 2027 may reflect the surge in corporate borrowing that has taken place to fund AI investment. Strong capex has come in part at the expense of buybacks, according to Goldman Sachs Research. That may create opportunities in “buyback aristocrats”—stocks with strong free cash flow generation and a commitment to returning cash to shareholders. During the past few decades, periods of slowing earnings and economic growth have favored stocks with price momentum, upward earnings revisions, and "quality" attributes such as low volatility and strong balance sheets, Snider writes. He says the information technology and healthcare sectors have a history of outperformance in these situations. Investors may also benefit from diversifying into defensive stocks, such as consumer staples companies, that tend to deliver stable profits even when the economy slows, according to Snider. “Although our base case is for continued earnings growth and equity market appreciation, the downside risks associated with extended earnings and valuations argue for diversifying portfolios with select defensives,” he writes. Our ranking of the Top 10 Stocks to Buy According to Billionaire Ken Fisher is out, and The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. (NYSE:GS) came in at number 9. Ken Fisher has spent more than four decades betting that big, globally dominant companies keep winning, and his latest filing shows he still believes it. His market call heading into the midterms was unambiguous. In an October interview, he said midterm years kick off what he considers the most consistently positive nine-month stretch in U.S. stock market history, because political gridlock blocks controversial legislation. In his words, The stock markets celebrate when major bills fall through. The filing backs that optimism. Across the firm's 10 largest stock positions, Fisher added shares to every one in the third quarter, and the notable cut came in bonds: he trimmed his 7-10 year Treasury bond fund by about 22%, a move consistent with a manager leaning into stocks rather than hiding in bonds. To build the list, we went through Fisher Asset Management's 13F for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, excluded options and ETFs, and ranked the 10 stocks with the largest share of the portfolio by stake value. Goldman Sachs qualified with a stake worth $6.38 billion, or 1.83% of the portfolio. Fisher added about 1.7% in the quarter, taking his position to roughly 7.08 million shares. Goldman Sachs is among Fisher's largest financial holdings, and it is a direct bet on the bull market he expects. When stocks rise and deals pick up, Goldman's trading desks and advisory business earn more. Its third-quarter results, reported in mid-October, delivered exactly that. Net revenue rose 23% to $18.68 billion, net earnings climbed about 29% to $5.29 billion, and diluted EPS rose to $17.01 from $12.25 a year earlier. Equities revenue jumped 72% to $6.44 billion, and asset and wealth management revenue rose 14% to $5.05 billion. CEO David Solomon said, Against the backdrop of a complicated operating environment, our clients continued to turn to Goldman Sachs for our world-class advice, execution and financing capabilities The flip side is that Goldman's earnings swing with markets. Revenue fell 8% compared to the previous quarter, a reminder that profits, based on trading, can fade quickly if volatility or deal activity cools. title: GS Caltex Overcomes Delay, Secures Sole Lead - 조선일보
content: 20-Minute Halt for Emergency Patient; GS Caltex Wins 3-1, Tops Standings [OSEN=Cho Hyung-rae Reporter] The match was delayed for about 20 minutes due to an emergency patient during the game, leading to a chaotic continuation. GS Caltex defeated Heungkuk Life Insurance. GS Caltex won 3-1 (25-19, 25-20, 18-25, 25-23) in the ‘2026-2027 HK Financial Group V-League Women’s Division’ match against Heungkuk Life Insurance held at the Incheon Samsan World Gymnasium on the 19th. With this victory, GS Caltex extended its winning streak to three games, recording 4 wins, 1 loss, and 12 points. It tied with the Industrial Bank of Korea (IBK) and Korea Expressway Corporation on points (4 wins, 1 loss each) but took sole first place by leading in set ratio. Heungkuk Life Insurance suffered its third consecutive loss, with 6 points (2 wins, 3 losses). GS Caltex dominated the first and second sets. In the first set, trailing 12-13, Tana scored two points from serves, and Silva successfully scored consecutive open attacks. Combined with Heungkuk Life Insurance’s touch net error, GS Caltex reversed the momentum to lead 18-13. The second set was also tightly contested, but with the score tied 17-17, Kwon Min-ji scored a blocking point. Heungkuk Life Insurance’s touch net error, Kim Hyo-im’s serve point, and Silva’s open attack gave GS Caltex the upper hand. However, an unexpected situation occurred in the third set. Heungkuk Life Insurance took control early. Leading 5-4, Jastis’s quick open attack, Jung Ho-young’s block, followed by Jung Ho-young’s quick spike and serve points, extended the lead to 9-5. Kindelan, Jastis, and Jung Ho-young’s points, along with Kindelan’s serve point, helped Heungkuk Life Insurance fend off GS Caltex’s comeback. Then, with Heungkuk Life Insurance leading 19-14 in the third set, an emergency patient occurred in the first-floor spectator area near the main office. The match was immediately halted, and on-site medical staff were deployed. After about 20 minutes of emergency treatment, including the arrival of 119 paramedics, the patient was transported to the hospital. The match resumed at 8:43 p.m., and Heungkuk Life Insurance won the third set. In the fourth set, GS Caltex overturned the tight battle. Yu Seo-yeon’s open attack tied the score at 22-23, followed by Kim Hyo-im’s serve point to reach 24-23 and secure the match point. Oh Se-yeon’s open attack completed the victory. GS Caltex had four players score double digits: Gisele Silva with 22 points, Choi Ga-eun with 12, Tana with 12, and Kwon Min-ji with 11. Heungkuk Life Insurance’s Kindelan scored 35 points, and Jung Ho-young added 14, but they failed to stop the losing streak at home. /jhrae@osen.co.kr

title: GS Caltex beats Heungkuk Life to take sole lead after match delay - Chosunbiz
content: The match was chaotic, with play delayed for about 20 minutes after a medical emergency. GS Caltex defeated Heungkuk Life. GS Caltex beat Heungkuk Life 3-1 (25-19, 25-20, 18-25, 25-23) in a women's match in the 2026-27 HK Heungkuk Finance V-League at Samsan World Gymnasium in Incheon on the 19th. GS Caltex extended its winning streak to three games and moved to 4-1 with 12 points, tying IBK Industrial Bank of Korea and Korea Expressway Corporation (KEC), also 4-1, but took sole possession of first place on set differential. Heungkuk Life fell to its third straight loss, leaving it with six points (2-3). GS Caltex controlled the first two sets. In the first set, after trailing 13-12, Tanacha scored two aces and Silva followed with consecutive kills. Heungkuk Life's errors helped GS Caltex turn the match around and take an 18-13 lead. The second set was also closely contested, but at 17-17, Kwon Min-ji scored a block point. A net-touching error by the opposition, Kim Hyo-im's ace and a kill by Silva, followed by a string of opponent errors, helped GS Caltex seize control. But an unexpected situation arose in the third set, which swung in Heungkuk Life's favor. Early in the set, with Heungkuk Life leading 5-4, Justice scored on a quick attack and Jung Ho-young blocked a shot. Jung then added a quick attack and an ace to help build a 9-5 lead. Points from Kindelan, Justice and Jung, along with an ace by Kindelan, helped Heungkuk Life fend off GS Caltex's rally. With Heungkuk Life leading 19-14 in the third set, a spectator suffered a medical emergency in the first-floor stands near the press box. Play was stopped immediately, and medical staff came onto the court to treat the person. Emergency responders also arrived. Play was delayed for about 20 minutes while first aid was administered, and the person was then taken to a hospital. The match resumed at 8:43 p.m., and Heungkuk Life claimed the third set. GS Caltex ultimately rallied to win a tightly contested fourth set. After Yoo Seo-yeon's kill tied the score at 23-23, Kim Hyo-im scored an ace to give the team a 24-23 match point. Oh Se-yeon then finished the win with a kill. GS Caltex had four players score in double figures: Gisele Silva with 22 points, Choi Ga-eun and Tanacha with 12 each, and Kwon Min-ji with 11. Kindelan scored 35 points and Jung Ho-young added 14 for Heungkuk Life, but the team could not stop its losing streak at home.

title: GS Motos Starts Benelli TNT25N Production - MEXICONOW
content:
Benelli and GS Motos have taken another step forward in their industrial strategy in Mexico with the start of production of the Benelli TNT25N at GS Motos’ manufacturing plant in Toluca. The model joins the Benelli 180S and TNT150, which began production in July, further strengthening the brand’s presence within GS Motos’ local manufacturing operations. The launch follows the introduction of models from Hero Motos, Benelli, and Morbidelli in 2026. With operations in Toluca and Guadalajara, GS Motos is strengthening its multi-brand manufacturing strategy and expanding its production capabilities in the Mexican market. “For GS Motos, assembling the Benelli TNT25N in Mexico means much more than simply bringing production closer to the market. It means combining the experience and discipline of local teams with a motorcycle that retains the brand’s sporty character and Italian inspiration. This new assembly operation reflects our confidence in GS Motos’ manufacturing capabilities and in the talent that makes each unit possible,” said Jorge García Puente, Director of Global Operations at GS Motos. The TNT25N production line operates at a rate of 34 units per hour, equivalent to approximately one motorcycle every 1.8 minutes. This pace is supported by a synchronized production process involving personnel, standardized procedures, and quality controls, with each station ensuring the precision and quality required for continuous production. The GS Motos manufacturing plant in Toluca has an annual production capacity of 1.2 million motorcycles. Since beginning operations in 2008, the facility has manufactured more than 10 million units. The start of TNT25N assembly further strengthens the role of the Toluca facility as a strategic manufacturing hub for GS Motos in Latin America. With the addition of the TNT25N, GS Motos is expanding its assembly capabilities in Mexico by incorporating another model into its multi-brand manufacturing operations. The move highlights the flexibility of its infrastructure and the expertise of its teams in producing motorcycles from different brands according to specific standards and requirements. The model’s integration into Mexican production lines also supports the development of skilled talent by combining Italian-inspired motorcycle design with the technical expertise of GS Motos’ local workforce. GS Caltex and Lee Young-taek, who won three consecutive games, expressed their feelings about the game. Coach Lee Young-taek looked back on the game in an interview after beating Heungkuk Life Insurance 3-1 in the first round of the "HK Heungkuk Finance 2026-2027 V-League" at Samsan World Gymnasium in Incheon on the 19th. He said, "The first and second sets went well, but the atmosphere went over from the third set. Yoo So-yeon, who entered the fourth set as a substitute, and Kim Hyo-im, who entered the last set, did a good job "I was able to win three points," he said. On this day, GS Caltex started with two outside heaters, Kwon Min-ji and Tanacha. In the fourth set, Yoo So-yeon replaced Tanacha, and Yoo So-yeon led the team to victory with 6 points, recording an attack success rate of 85.71% in the fourth set alone. Coach Lee said, "Tanacha's receiving was shaken, and his offensive rhythm was not good. He said he put in a suicide note to give something to give to the opponent and to have a sense of stability on our side. Silva, who scored the most 22 points in the team, used a mixture of standing serve and spike serve when serving. In this regard, he said, "I have a little muscle pain in my back, and I have a burden on my knees and ankles, so I did it in the sense of controlling myself. Then a miss came out. If the serve goes well, it is difficult for the opponent to receive it, but there were many mistakes. If there are many mistakes, you can change your serve on your own. I'm not talking too much about this. He explained, "I'm controlling it on my own." Silva also complained of back discomfort in the last game. Coach Lee explained, "My back was a little uncomfortable before that, but it's not that I can't play or train." On the same day, GS Caltex's Silva took 36.36% of the attack share, followed by Tanacha with 25%, Kwon Min-ji with 15.91%, and Choi Ga-eun with 12.12%. It was a departure from the criticism that the "bread and bread" against Silva was severe. In this regard, head coach Lee Young-taek said with force, "I'm telling you again, it's not that everything is bad." "If you have the ability, you have to use it," he continued, adding, "Tanacha and Kwon Min-ji also came up, so I think the setter trusts the players and distributes them evenly. That is the judgment of setter Kim Ji-won. title: GS Engineering & Construction expands housing beyond physical space - Chosunbiz
content: GS Engineering & Construction reimagines apartment living with Xi services The construction industry's approach to selling homes is shifting from simply providing "floor space" to "designing daily life" for residents. Xi (XI), the flagship residential brand of GS Engineering & Construction, is also moving beyond the traditional role of a builder that constructs physical structures, transforming itself into a "Life Enabler" that supports residents throughout their day. In today's housing market, the quality of the amenities and living experience residents can enjoy after moving in is considered a key competitive advantage, rather than physical specifications such as the size of individual units or residential complexes. In line with that trend, GS Engineering & Construction plans to bring together complex design, community spaces, advanced technology and lifestyle services to introduce a new residential culture that extends from individuals to families and neighbors. The most immediately noticeable change is an artificial intelligence (AI)-based living environment that saves residents "time." Through its "AI Home" ecosystem, developed in partnership with LG Electronics, Xi actively manages the home environment without residents having to intervene. From the time residents wake up until they go to bed, it tracks their biological rhythms and movements around the home and automatically adjusts lighting, temperature and ventilation. It seamlessly controls appliances such as washing machines and vacuum cleaners, as well as curtains, and switches modes for activities such as relaxing after returning home or watching a movie, all without separate manual controls. By relieving residents of the burden of tedious housework and device management, AI allows them to devote their personal time to activities such as talking with family or pursuing hobbies. The unconventional flexibility of the "space" also stands out. GS Engineering & Construction has introduced "Moving Wall," a flexible furnishing that uses Robotics technology to divide or combine interior spaces as needed. In one representative configuration, the "Hidden Kitchen," a wall moves on its own without a rail to conceal the kitchen when it is not in use. The extra space can then be turned into a home workout room, study or hobby room. Rather than being confined to the floor plan set when residents move in, the home effectively transforms itself as a family's life stage and lifestyle change. The company has also invested in landscaping and community design to ensure residents can enjoy uninterrupted "rest" in the city. Alongside "Club Xian," a community facility reserved for residents, it has created nature-friendly relaxation spaces, including a central woodland, water garden and tea house, so residents can recharge without traveling far. To prepare for worsening climate change in particular, the company will gradually introduce "housing solutions for responding to the climate crisis" across its complexes, developed in collaboration with a research team led by professor Carlo Ratti at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Senseable City Lab. It has created comfortable complexes regardless of the season or outside weather through cooling fog systems that reduce fine dust, specialized landscaping that mitigates the urban heat island effect and energy-self-sufficient, environmentally friendly facilities. The effort to make daily life more "convenient" is rounded out by combining premium food and beverage services with a digital platform. GS Engineering & Construction has partnered with food and beverage (F&B) brand "Gourmet de Galleria" to gradually introduce a dining service on par with that of a luxury hotel, offering breakfast, brunch and a premium cafeteria within its complexes. The aim is to ease the work of preparing meals and cleaning up during busy mornings. The company has also linked the services to a smartphone app exclusively for Xi residents, allowing them to easily request concierge services, register visiting vehicles and control devices in their homes. A GS Engineering & Construction representative said, "Apartments are no longer just assets or walls to live within. They are becoming multifaceted platforms that enrich residents' daily lives and lifestyles." The representative added, "GS Engineering & Construction's Xi will lead the way in residential culture, drawing on Moving Wall, premium F&B, AI smart homes and climate-responsive design to help residents enjoy a completely different level of living within their complexes."

title: ESPN’s Jimmy Pitaro on the New Playbook for Sports Fans - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Analysis and forecasts on global economies and markets for the year ahead from economists and strategists across Goldman Sachs. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. The launch of ESPN’s direct-to-consumer service a year ago was a marker of change in the sports media business—offering the full suite of ESPN networks without a pay-TV bundle for the first time. ESPN Chairman Jimmy Pitaro joins Dave Dase, global co-head of the Sports franchise in Investment Banking, and discusses how this challenging decision helps the company reach younger viewers and “serve the sports fan anytime, anywhere.” Pitaro also talks about the strength of ESPN’s current sports rights portfolio, why the company is sometimes willing to walk away from media rights negotiations, and explains how AI allows ESPN to create new offerings. Jimmy Pitaro:     The foundation of ESPN is live events. Everything that we do, original content, our 30 for 30, E60, SC Featured, our studio programming. It all is built off of that foundation of live games. Dave Dase:   Good afternoon. Welcome to Talks at GS. I'm Dave Dase. I head up our Southeast business and co-head our global sports business in investment banking. I'm joined today by Jimmy Pitaro, chairman of ESPN, who's led one of the most important transitions in sports media. Under Jimmy's leadership, ESPN launched its full direct-to-consumer streaming service, expanded its partnership with the NFL, and continued reshaping how fans watch, follow, and engage with sports, all of which we will discuss today. Jimmy, you signed and closed a deal with the NFL on Red Zone NFL Network earlier this year. Maybe just talk about the impact that's having, right, as you think about broadly NFL football. Jimmy Pitaro:     Well, let me first say thank you for the partnership on that. You were involved in that in that deal. We feel great about it. For those of you that don't know really what we're talking about, we acquired the NFL Network. ESPN did. We also acquired their entire fantasy business. We acquired their Red Zone linear business, and we acquired the Red Zone brand. In exchange, the league took a 10% equity stake in ESPN. Walt Disney Company owns the majority. We have another shareholder, Hearst. And now we have the NFL at 10%. The relationship with the league, I think, has never been better. I think they're very pleased with the deal. We're very pleased with the deal. We've now ingested NFL Network into the ESPN app, which I'm sure you want to talk about. But now if you're a subscriber to our premium tier called ESPN Unlimited, you have access to all the programming of NFL Network. We are, as I said before, the official game, the official fantasy game of the NFL. So, we've combined those two products. Many of you probably saw this. We had a US Open Red Zone, which filled me with joy. It was exactly what I was envisioning when we were negotiating this deal with the league and looking to acquire that Red Zone brand. Not just the linear product, but the Red Zone brand. What else could we do with that brand? We kicked it off with the US Open. We're looking at other opportunities. Potentially college football, although we haven't decided on that yet. That's something that's on the board. But we're in really good shape here with this deal. And we're excited about what it means for the future at ESPN. Dave Dase:   Maybe talk about a year ago you launched the direct-to-consumer platform and streaming platform. That was a tough decision. Something that was talked about in, you know, the ecosystem for many, many years, for you as well as other, certainly the other more traditional or legacy broadcast cable-oriented type businesses. But talk a little bit about that process, what your goals and objectives were, and just how it's performed thus far. Jimmy Pitaro:     You nailed it. It was a really tough decision. And the entire industry was focused on it. What is this going to mean? If ESPN goes direct-to-consumer over the top, what is that going to mean for cord cutting? Are all sports fans then going to cancel their paid TV subscription? We knew that wouldn't happen. I mean, we have, call it high-level, maybe one-third of the market from a sports viewership perspective. We don't have everything. We can't have everything. It doesn't work for us. From our perspective, knowing that it wasn't going to cause a total collapse of paid television, which has been very good to ESPN and the Walt Disney Company. It's a fantastic business model for us. We had to be very careful in terms of when we were going to actually go direct-to-consumer. And I spent many, many hours in a conference room with Bob Iger on this topic. And so, ultimately, we made the call that we would go summer of 2025. And so, we did it in August of last year. So, we just celebrated our one-year anniversary. Look, our strategy was what I often refer to as parallel paths. Meaning how do we make ourselves available to people who are not interested in paid television? Okay? Mostly the younger generation, but there are others my age that are just not interested in paid television anymore. We need to be there. Our mission is to serve the sports fan anytime, anywhere. And so, if you're not interested in paid television, we still need ESPN to be accessible to you. Okay, so we're going to go direct-to-consumer. At the same time, as I said before, paid television has been really important to us in our bottom line. And so, how do we go direct-to-consumer and protect that legacy or traditional business? And so, what we ended up doing, and this was a very challenging decision and somewhat of a polarizing topic early on in the discussions, we decided to make ESPN DTC available to all paid TV subscribers long-term. Ultimately, now we have to get the deals done with the distributors, but the vast majority of distributors today are now offering what we call entitlements. Meaning, if you're a subscriber to Charter, Comcast, YouTube TV, Hulu Live. You fire up the ESPN app. You enter your credentials and you get access to everything ESPN direct-to-consumer. So, what does that mean? That was our way of adding value to paid TV. So, we went direct-to-consumer. We're available there as an option. But if you're a paid TV subscriber, that subscription is far more valuable to you than it was yesterday. Two things. Timing. We knew we were going to go direct-to-consumer. It was a matter of when, not if. And do we offer these entitlements to paid TV subscribers? And the answer to that one was yes. Dave Dase:   Great. Let's talk a little bit about media rights. From my sense, the comprehensive best content out there, you probably have the strongest portfolio today as you've ever had. How do you think about the value proposition of what rights do you want? How do you think of return on investment? Jimmy Pitaro:     I get this question all the time. It's probably where I spend the most amount of time dealing with rights. The foundation of ESPN is live events. Everything that we do, original content, our 30 for 30, E60, SC Featured, our studio programming. It all is built off of that foundation of live games. And so, thank you for acknowledging that. Yes, our rights portfolio today, we're 47 years old at ESPN. And it's the best it's ever been. It's the best that the industry has ever seen from any one enterprise. So, we feel really good about that. At the same time, as I mentioned before, we cannot have everything. It just would not work for us financially. We spend just as much time analyzing things that we end up passing on as things that we end up acquiring. But we sit down, we do the analysis. We have a very sophisticated rights acquisitions team, a very sophisticated strategy team, finance team. We all get together. We look at value to pay television. Are the affiliates interested in this content? We look at projected ratings and corresponding ad sales. And then we look at value on the direct-to-consumer side. And then we make the best offer that we can. But we're at peace. If the league or the conference is looking for something significantly more, we're at peace with walking away. All that said, Dave, I still really like our hand. Historically, we're competing against NBC, CBS, and Fox. Today, we're still competing against the incumbents. And yet we're competing against Netflix, YouTube, Amazon, Apple, DAZN. And so, it's fiercely competitive. But I said I like our hand. And the reason why I said that is because we're the Walt Disney Company. And so, when we sit down at the table, we don't just bring ESPN linear. We bring everything that I mentioned before digitally. We bring broadcast through ABC. We bring Hulu. We bring Disney Plus. We bring the power of the theme parks for promotion. And so, I'm not quite sure a league or a conference is going to get that kind of value. We also bring the megaphone that is ESPN. We're the only folks that are covering sports every day, all day long, 365. We are in a really good place here because that portfolio that you mentioned, it's locked up. Like, for the next, I don't know, five to 10 years, we're in really good shape because those rights are spoken for now. Dave Dase:   Yeah. It seems like you have an interesting rights decision to make with respect to the college football playoff. Maybe talk about there's been an explosion in terms of sports valuations. We've certainly seen that. Women's sports, people are really talking about. There's real capital going into. And I often get asked the question by clients or investors or people who may want to buy a team, you know, what's going on? Why is this different now with women's sports? I give you and ESPN a lot of credit for - women's sports needed oxygen. And you, in some ways, were the oxygen, which gave distribution platform both at the college level as well as at the professional level. But talking about that. Was that intentional? Was it part of the strategy? How did you think about women's sports and how are you thinking about it today? Because it's a fantastic moment for, you know, both of us have daughters. And many of you, right, you have daughters who are playing sports and everything else. It's a fantastic time. Jimmy Pitaro:     Thank you for recognizing that. I can take zero credit for ESPN's investment in women's sports. It long predates me. This has been a multi-decade priority at the company. I mean, we were the WNBA launch partner 30 years ago. We've had the NCAA women's tournament for decades, which is a crown jewel in our portfolio. But I will tell you that, you know, over the past decade, we have significantly increased our investment in women's sports, both professional and college. You know, we now have a fantastic partnership with the NWSL. We have a partnership with Athletes Unlimited on the softball side, which we love. That's another sport that's on fire. Women's volleyball is on fire. Everything volleyball is up and to the right. We're also, as an extension of the live games, we're investing in women's fantasy. Fantasy is a big part of our DNA at ESPN. We have significantly more women's studio programming today than we did a decade ago. We love the fact that the industry is kind of working with us here. It's not just ESPN. Others are clearly-- our competitors are clearly making investments as well. And what we're seeing is this rising tide. And last thing I'd say on this is the dollars are following. Like advertisers, sponsors are very focused on women's sports. So, fandom is heading that way. And so are the dollars. So, it makes perfect sense for us on a variety of levels to be increasing our investments. Dave Dase:   Incredibly competitive, right, areas to be in, in and of themselves. What was your approach? For a sports fan out there, they would say, gosh, you have the dream job, right? Running ESPN. But what was your approach just from a career development kind of advice? Or how did you get to where you got to? Or, you know, what sort of skill set got you there? Jimmy Pitaro:     Well, I am, as you are, I'm a crazy sports fan. My wife thinks I need therapy on this. Like, I'm not exaggerating when I say my mood is completely dependent on how the Yankees do like the next day and how Notre Dame football does. My whole life has been team sports. Dave and I also played together. And so, I know you can relate to this, but my whole life, I've just loved team sports. By the way, this started at Edgemont High School in Scarsdale, New York, which is where your CEO went. David's younger brother was my classmate at Edgemont High School. And he was a friend of mine. But my fandom, my crazy fandom, I was surrounded by crazy sports fans. My mom does not watch it when the Yankees are in the field because she thinks nothing good can happen when the Yankees are in the field. Like that's how crazy-- My sister is the general counsel of Major League Baseball. Like I'm surrounded by crazy sports-- all of my friends, we used to leave Edgemont High School and go to the Bronx and sit in the bleachers. So, my crazy fandom started then. You know, played in college. And you know, my fandom just continued to grow. I was a lawyer. I learned a ton. I went to law school and practiced. I was a litigator for several years. Learned a ton on the litigation side, really starting with like public speaking and the importance of brevity. But yes, then I made the transition to the business side at Yahoo and got immersed in technology. That was a blessing for me. Everyone has breaks during their careers. And so, when I was asked to leave law and run a business, it was Yahoo Sports. I went from managing 12 people to managing over a thousand people overnight, most of whom were technicians, engineers, front end, back end engineers, designers. I'm this lawyer guy managing these folks. And that was quite daunting. But baptism by fire. I learned a ton. By the way, I was competing with ESPN every day of my life. I woke up every day and challenged the team, how are we going to beat ESPN? Anyway, I met Bob Iger, Steve Jobs, who I'd worked with, and Sheryl Sandberg, who I knew very well, were on the Disney board. They were looking to make a change. Bob was looking to make a change on the digital side. That's actually how I joined the Walt Disney Company, not to run ESPN, but to lead Disney Interactive, their digital horizontal business. It doesn't exist anymore today. But because of my Yahoo days and being immersed in technology, I was able to take a lot of that learning and be effective at Disney Interactive. And then in 2017, the gentleman who was running ESPN resigned. Working for Bob was such a blessing. Every year during my review with Bob, he would ask me, or we would have a conversation around what I wanted to do next and would always end with ESPN. So, fast forward to 2017, the ESPN job opens up and Bob calls me, "I'm assuming you want this?" I said, "Yes." And then I had to interview 16 times. I had an interview with the entire board and several people in corporate. Anyway, ended up getting the job. And it's been a dream. Dave Dase:   Talk a little bit about your management style today, sitting on top of this organization all over the world, 24-7, 365. You have massive personalities, right, in the media business. You have best-in-class innovative technology. What's your management style? How do you handle this? Jimmy Pitaro:     I just love being a part of a team. I really do. And so, the highlight of my week is my senior staff meeting. All of my direct reports and I get together, and we sit in our ESPN boardroom, and I say, "Discuss, debate, decide a line." And so, our chief of staff puts together the agenda. And we have real tough debates. She'll tee up the discussion and we will debate. And my direct reports know that not only can they challenge me, but I'm still learning. Every single day, I'm trying to learn and be an effective leader, but I want to be, I need to be challenged. I don't just want yes people around me. We have really healthy discussion and debate. And then we try to decide as a team. We don't get paralyzed by the analysis. We try to decide as a team. And more often than not, far more often than not, we do. But there are times where we can't agree. And so, then I make the decision. That's what I'm getting paid to do. And then the most important part of that is alignment, right? Once the decision is made, and I feel really strongly about this, and I've had some roadblocks in my career on this last one, but as a leader at the Walt Disney Company and ESPN, you lose the luxury of questioning the decision after it's been made. Right? You want a forum to be heard. And you have that at ESPN. But once we make the decision, or I make the decision, then the expectation is alignment, even if you were in the minority, you didn't agree with the decision. You asked me what my leadership philosophy is. There are several components to that. But at a macro level, I think that's the most important thing I would call out. Dave Dase:   We talked a little bit about artificial intelligence. As you sit here today, as we sit here today, what do you think it's like being a fan 10 years from now, 20 years from now? Where does this innovation go? I had this debate with some team owners around, is there ultimately a physical sporting world and, you know, a completely digital, in essence, sporting world that coexists, overlapped to some extent? But just with AI and everything else, where do you think this goes? And I will say, right, most of the owners who are calling, or most people who want to deploy capital - institutions, individuals, billionaires who want to deploy capital into sports teams, are now, at least for the last 9 or 12 months, saying it's a hedge on AI. Right? Dave Dase:   People want to be there. It's a true hedge. It's an asset allocation play. And I think, in large part, I mean, we've seen some pretty significant uptick in sports valuations. And so, I think part of that, you know, is from that. But just how do you think about AI and where does this go and what's it like to be a fan? Jimmy Pitaro:     My old boss contributed to that increase. Dave Dase:   He did. He did, yes. Teams are being bought, not sold. Jimmy Pitaro:     Yeah. Everyone's talking about AI today, of course. We've been invested in AI for many, many years at ESPN. And so, the SportsCenter For You that I mentioned before would not exist without AI. But for us, AI has been nothing but a blessing. And for the sports fan, from my perspective, it's been nothing but a blessing. It hasn't displaced jobs. Okay? If anything, it's helping our business grow so that we can hire more people. Like, that's how I look at it. But examples outside of SportsCenter For You? Highlights. Highlight generation. Like, a lot of that is being generated through AI. We can generate far more highlights at scale than we ever could before. We talked about women's sports, but some of the smaller leagues, like the Premier Lacrosse League, NWSL, TGL, we can now do game recaps that are automatically generated. Now, we can't go out and hire 5,000 people to create game recaps. It just would not be cost effective for us. We're running a business. But now, through AI, and it's not always perfect, but we can generate game recaps. Investigative reporting. I talk about this all the time. My commute to Bristol, Connecticut, sometimes I'm in the car for an hour and a half. And so, our investigative reports oftentimes could take you 30, 45 minutes to read. They're very lengthy and in-depth. And I don't have the time to get through all of that. So, now, you can just tap on the Listen button and the narration is automatically generated. I expect to see a lot more of that. In terms of your point on sports being somewhat AI-proof, I do agree with that for the most part. Again, full circle, I think AI is going to do nothing but-- not just for ESPN, but for the industry, is going to improve the experience. Whether it's in stadium - we all know what's happening now with places like Cosm. Like, that whole experience is off the charts great from my perspective. And I think that's just going to continue to improve. Dave Dase:   Well, thank you very much. Thanks for being a client. Thanks for being so generous with your time. Most importantly, thanks for providing all this content that makes everybody's lives so interesting. Jimmy Pitaro:     Thank you for having me, everybody. Appreciate it. TITUSVILLE — Aerospace pioneer Draper wants to spin missile parts around really fast on the Space Coast, and on Tuesday it opened the doors of a new 51,010-square-foot facility to do just that. The biggest facet is a 70-foot-diameter room that will house a centrifuge capable of spinning up to 4,900 pounds of payloads up to 25 G’s. That’s 48 rotations per minute, which could hurl the 33-foot-long centrifuge arm to more than 113 mph. “In a word. Terrifying,” said Draper program manager Joe Bucci, who has been working on the site for three years. He showed off the cavernous room with his voice echoing off the curved walls. One tiny window separated it from the planned control center where he said people looking through won’t even have time to react. “Every time if goes by, your body wants to flinch back.” For now, the stark white room simply has circular lights on the ceiling reminiscent of a scene from “Tron,” with only the massive letters of the company’s name stenciled on the wall. It’s the marquee item of the building, named the Strategic Enhanced Ground Test Facility, that also has seven specialized test cells all within a structure designed to keep things classified. Guidance and navigation systems would be the main test subject, put through the rigors that simulate what they might endure if part of a missile, rocket or spacecraft. “As far as the whole package, it’s the best in the world,” Bucci said. The majority of Draper’s work is dedicated to supporting the military, but it also has had a hand helping NASA. Draper’s guidance systems were used for Apollo missions and are still part of the Artemis program today. Draper CEO and President Jerry Wohletz said the new facility represents the company’s investment in the nation’s strategic capability. “Rigorous testing is a crucial component of Draper’s engineering process and ensures that the systems our nation is building will work as intended and do so under the conditions they will face in the real world,” he said. The main centrifuge will be a monster driven by four motors using 500 megawatts to propel the arm. “And good news for our neighbors: there is a 2-foot-thick reinforced concrete wall in the event of a mishap to protect the neighborhood and the surrounding area,” he said. The centrifuge isn’t expected to become active until 2028, with its primary customer, the Naval Ordnance Test Unit based in Cape Canaveral, eager for its arrival. Draper has been supplying guidance systems for Navy missiles since 1955. U.S. Navy Vice Admiral Douglas Williams, director of Portfolio Acquisition Executive Strategic Systems Programs, was on hand for the opening ceremony Tuesday. “Every fleet ballistic missile deployed by the Navy, from Polaris A1 to Trident II D5, has been equipped with a guidance system designed by Draper. The unmatched reliability, accuracy and survivability of our sea-launched deterrent would not exist without this vital partnership,” he said. He said the new complex will help the Navy move quickly through design and validation for its weapon systems, which have the NOTU facilities at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station and Port Canaveral as the primary testing ground. NOTU has about 185 civilian and enlisted personnel. “This building and the team it will house support a no-fail mission,” he said. “The sea-based deterrent is the backbone of our nation’s defense.” Draper was founded as an independent nonprofit organization at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 1933. It has been doing centrifuge testing at an aging facility that was built at Hanscom Air Force Base in Bedford, Mass., in 1956. But Florida won out over Massachusetts when Draper debated building its replacement. “This building directly addresses the need for the defense industrial base to recapitalize aging infrastructure and build new specialized infrastructure to support future capabilities,” Williams said. “Make no mistake about it, folks: when I communicate to the Chief of Naval Operations, I tell him our biggest risk is infrastructure. And you guys just proved, through your resolve, that we can tackle it and we can overcome it.” Company officials said choosing the Space Coast had the benefit of proximity to its customers including the Navy, Air Force, Missile Defense Agency and NASA, as well as access to the growing aerospace talent pool in the region. It joins an aerospace landscape in northern Brevard County that includes thousands employed by the likes of launch companies like SpaceX and Blue Origin. The $74 million building has been in the works since 2023 with groundbreaking happening as Florida was being hit by Hurricane Idalia. Work will still begin at the building for now with a small staff, but one that will grow to at least 50 high-paying jobs in the short-term, marking Draper’s first sustained presence on the Space Coast. It has about 2,900 employees at 20 locations across the U.S., but the company’s plans have it growing to 3,500 by the 2030s, including growing its Brevard County staff to 150. While still a nonprofit, it had more than $1 billion in revenue in 2025. Titusville Mayor Andrew Connors toured the facility and welcomed it as a diverse, but lucrative addition to the region’s economic base. “For a long time, we were always the place to launch rockets, but now we’ve finally developed that supply chain for assembly, manufacturing, and this is a critical component of that, which is research and development,” he said. ” So we’re very, very excited to bring that entire supply chain right here in North Brevard.” He said what Draper is offering helps cushion the region from economic woes it has experienced in the past, such as the end of the Space Shuttle Program in 2011. “I think there’s some changes that we need to make strategically to make sure that we don’t run into another recession, because if you look at the history of Titusville, it’s filled with the booms and busts of space, and it impacts North Brevard far more than it impacts the rest of the county,” he said, While the launch rate seems like it will keep the Space Coast busy over the next decade, Florida might not always be in such a prominent position. “We need to focus on that entire supply chain, as well as diversifying, learning those lessons from 2011, and just setting ourselves up for success 20 years from now,” Connors said. “Because there’s more and more competition out there. You see SpaceX buying thousands of acres in Louisiana, Texas. Once the FAA clears the ability to launch and land rockets over people, are we special?” Subscribers are entitled to 10 gift sharing articles each month. title: Oil Is Estimated to Ease in 2027 as Suppliers Adapt to Hormuz Disruption - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Analysis and forecasts on global economies and markets for the year ahead from economists and strategists across Goldman Sachs. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Oil is forecast to ease gradually in 2027 as suppliers in the Middle East adapt to disruption from the war in Iran, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Our commodities analysts expect benchmark Brent crude to average $88 per barrel in 2027 under their base case assumption of no definitive diplomatic breakthrough in Iran and no re-escalation with major long-term damage to oil infrastructure. Under the same base case scenario, they project that Brent will fall from $93 per barrel today (as of November 17) to $78 by early December 2027 as a sizable surplus decreases Brent’s fair value from $90 per barrel today to the high $70s by the end of 2027. Goldman Sachs Research expects the risk premium in oil prices—which now appears relatively low—to gradually normalize. Oil prices have risen less sharply this year than expected given the length of shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, writes Daan Struyven, co-head of global commodities research and head of oil research, in a report by his team. In part, that was because of “remarkable oil market adaptation” to the war in Iran, Struyven adds. This included Gulf exporters redirecting supply through pipelines, dark exports, US Navy escorts, and ship-to-ship transfers. The adaptation also included lower oil demand in response to higher prices—notably in China, which switched some of its energy demand to power and coal—and strong output of oil outside the Gulf, especially in Brazil. “For 2027, we again expect a contest between high supply disruption risk and continued market adaptation,” Struyven writes. The oil market likely tipped into a surplus in October 2026. The key driver was a rise in the supply of oil from the Persian Gulf in October—Goldman Sachs Research estimates that Persian Gulf crude exports recovered in October to their 2025 average, increasing 2 million barrels per day compared with the previous month. Under Goldman Sachs Research’s base case scenario, our analysts expect the surplus to grow in 2027. They estimate that it will reach 2 million barrels per day in 2027 despite slowing growth in output from outside the Persian Gulf and continued supply disruptions. Our analysts expect the recovery of output from the Gulf to trend higher as adaptation and added transportation resources, especially a larger tanker fleet and pipelines, support further growth in production. Goldman Sachs Research expects an additional 3.8mb/d of pipeline capacity to come online over the next year as oil producers in the Middle East invest in pipelines that bypass the Strait of Hormuz and transport oil directly to the Gulf of Oman, Red Sea, or Mediterranean Sea. Struyven’s base case assumption sees 2027 oil output from the Gulf exceeding its 2025 average by 1.4 million barrels per day. Global demand for oil took a hit from the conflict in the Middle East. Goldman Sachs Research expects global demand, with the exception of China, to recover to its pre-war trend once the availability and affordability of oil products improve, consistent with the rebounds in global demand following negative oil supply shocks in 2011 and 2022. In China, our analysts expect persistent weakness in road fuel oil demand to drive 0.4 million barrels per day of “scarring” to global oil demand by the fourth quarter of 2027. The surge in use of electric passenger cars and trucks likely accelerated China’s energy transition, helping drive a 0.7 million barrel-per-day drop in Chinese gasoline and diesel demand in September 2026, year over year. Half of that decline is likely to persist, according to Goldman Sachs Research. “Taken together, we estimate that China’s total oil demand peaked in 2025,” Struyven writes. Goldman Sachs Research’s base case assumption is for European liquefied natural gas (LNG) prices to average €45 per megawatt hour in 2027 as supply from the Middle East continues to adapt. That would represent a decline from €85/MWh today (as of November 17). “Yet even as supply adaptation has spread, it has worked less well for other commodities than for crude oil and has sharply raised shipping costs,” writes Samantha Dart, co-head of Global Commodities Research, who also leads the team’s global natural gas research. The complexities of transporting LNG, which needs to be kept at very cold temperatures, make ship-to-ship transfers harder than for oil. And because it is more flammable than oil, transporting LNG can be more dangerous for the crew in the event of an attack, Dart explains. European LNG could rise to near €150/MWh in the first quarter of 2027 if Persian Gulf LNG exports average 25%-30% of pre-war levels this winter and if Europe's winter turns out one standard deviation colder (0.7° Celsius) than average, Dart writes. If Gulf LNG exports stall at around 35% of pre-war levels through end-2027, her team estimates that European LNG prices would average €104/MWh in 2027. title: GS Yuasa discovers why moisture degrades sulfide solid-state electrolytes - www.bestmag.co.uk
content: GS Yuasa and Osaka Metropolitan University have identified how trace moisture reduces the ionic conductivity of sulfide solid electrolytes used in all-solid-state batteries. The Japanese battery manufacturer said the research could support development of more moisture-resistant sulfide electrolytes and manufacturing processes that better suppress degradation. Sulfide solid electrolytes are attractive for all-solid-state batteries because of their high ionic conductivity, but they are also sensitive to moisture. Exposure to even small quantities of water in the atmosphere can generate harmful hydrogen sulfide and reduce the electrolyte’s ability to conduct lithium ions. GS Yuasa said it had previously demonstrated that changing the composition of sulfide electrolytes could significantly suppress hydrogen sulfide generation, but the mechanism responsible for the loss of ionic conductivity had remained unclear. Researchers from GS Yuasa and the Inorganic Chemistry Group at Osaka Metropolitan University’s Graduate School of Engineering used solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance, or NMR, analysis to investigate what happens when moisture enters the electrolyte. Solid-state NMR allows researchers to examine the local chemical environment of atoms within solid materials. The team first observed how the NMR spectrum changed after a sulfide electrolyte was exposed to air containing trace amounts of moisture. Computational chemistry was then used to model electrolyte structures containing water and generate simulated NMR spectra. By comparing the simulations with experimental measurements, the researchers developed a method for distinguishing water present on the electrolyte surface from moisture that had entered the bulk material. They found that ionic conductivity fell as the amount of moisture inside the solid electrolyte increased. The result indicates that preventing water from penetrating the electrolyte itself could be important in maintaining performance, rather than focusing solely on surface reactions or hydrogen sulfide generation. Controlling moisture is an important manufacturing challenge for sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries because sensitive materials can require low-humidity or dry-room production environments, increasing process complexity and cost. BESTmag recently reported that QuantumScape’s Osprey platform combines a sulfide-based cathode with its ceramic separator, indicating a growing interest in sulfide materials for solid-state cells. Other manufacturers  developing sulfide-based technologies include Saft and Eve Energy. Saft recently opened solid-state battery production lines in Bordeaux capable of working with sulfide and polymer electrolytes, while Eve Energy is developing 60 Ah all-solid-state cells using sulfide and halide electrolyte systems. The GS Yuasa research forms part of Japan’s New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization Green Innovation Fund programme for advanced solid-state battery development. GS Yuasa has also completed installation of large-scale battery prototyping equipment at its Kyoto headquarters and has begun operating the facility. The company said it will use the findings from the moisture study to develop manufacturing processes for all-solid-state batteries as it moves towards full-scale operation of the prototyping equipment. Some of the research results are due to be presented at the 67th Battery Symposium in Japan on 24–26 November and at the 52nd Symposium on Solid State Ionics in Japan in December. title: Adam Goldston and Ryan Goldston on Defining Luxury Performance Footwear - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Analysis and forecasts on global economies and markets for the year ahead from economists and strategists across Goldman Sachs. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. When APL (Athletic Propulsion Labs) set out to create basketball shoes that helped athletes instantly jump higher, the technology worked so well that the NBA banned the shoes for providing the wearer with an undue competitive advantage. That sparked viral global demand for the shoes and propelled APL to success. Adam Goldston and Ryan Goldston, co-founders of APL, explain the “luxury performance” philosophy of their footwear, their strategies for growing their business, and how they drew design inspiration from ziplines and Japanese soufflé pancakes. In a conversation with Meena Flynn, chair of global Private Wealth Management and co-head of One Goldman Sachs, the Goldstons also articulate how the experience of running an independent, founder-owned firm, a focus on product, and flexible decision-making guide APL’s long-term growth and dynastic strategy. Adam Goldston:   There's not that many moments in your life when you realize, okay, this can be a defining moment, and everything can change based on what you do right now. Ryan Goldston:   We still feel like we're at the very beginning and there's all of this runway in front of us because of this dynastic lens that we've looked at the business and the brand through and also just the sheer opportunity that's in front of us. Meena Flynn:      I am Meena Flynn. I chair our global private wealth management business and I'm co-head of One Goldman Sachs. I am thrilled today to be joined by Adam and Ryan Goldston, co-founders and co-CEOs of APL, Athletic Propulsion Labs. They actually began the company when they were both two sport college athletes at Division I USC playing football and basketball. And APL was born from a business plan that one professor told them was doomed to fail. That being said, in 2010, the NBA banned their shoes, saying that their shoes created an unfair technology advantage. Since then, they built APL into a category defining brand at the center of sports, performance, and luxury. So, please join me in welcoming both Adam and Ryan today. So, let's start with the problem that you were trying to solve with APL. It came out of your needs living every day as college athletes and really wanting to jump higher, perform better, and push beyond whatever existing footwear could do. You began with technology and then really built the product around it. And so, when did you first set out to build and what gap were you trying to address? Ryan Goldston:   Adam and I are not six foot ten, as you guys can probably tell. And we both played basketball and football at USC. So, we were always focused on doing anything we could to increase our performance. But there was never anything that could make it so we could do it instantly. So, when I was an entrepreneurship program, I used APL as my business plan. And I said there are three things that were going to make it unique. One, we're going to create a shoe that instantly makes you jump higher. Two, we're going to price it at $300, which at the time was twice the price of anything else within the market. And three, we're going to start by selling direct to consumer. So, this is back in 2008/2009. DTC wasn't the same that it is now. Price points weren't where they are now. And there was never a shoe that instantly made you jump higher. So, what we did is we identified a category we wanted to create, which was luxury performance. We started in a micro niche where we had authenticity and credibility because we were college athletes. And we tried to create something that was for ourselves that we felt was not just a want, but a need from a performance standpoint and something that hadn't previously existed within the market. The fact that my professor at the time told me it'd be a massive failure. I didn't get top 10 in the business plan competition. And we actually started the company that I wrote in that business plan, was to us proof that we had something unique and different and that we were going to be able to create a category that was defining and that we could own. And so, I would say that it came out of a want and a need from us from a performance standpoint. We felt like we had a unique point of view that we were bringing to the market. And ultimately, we had groundbreaking technology that set the trajectory for us to create this category of luxury performance. Meena Flynn:      So, the NBA banned your shoes in 2010. Why did they ban your shoes? I mean, it became viral overnight. And how did you approach that situation? Adam Goldston:   So, that was probably the singular moment that changed our lives more than anything. When the NBA banned our concept one, because they said it provided the way with an undue competitive advantage over their opponents, that was the best thing that ever happened to us. So, we had created a singular product. And for us, like we believed in it because we made it for ourselves. But we were 22 at the time when it happened. So, we had finished college. We're in this small office. Created this revolutionary product. And when it happened, Ryan and I essentially looked at each other and said, we can either try and fight this, or we can lean into this. Keep in mind, we had zero marketing budget back then. So, we're in a way different situation today than we were then. Zero marketing budget and the difference back in 2010 versus today is news cycles were much longer. So, when these big moments happened, there was a much longer tail to them than it is today. So, now with the attention economy, if something goes viral or it's huge, it may last a couple of days if you're really lucky, but then it deteriorates very quickly. Back then, it was just continuing to go and compound for us. So, when it happened, Ryan and I were sitting in the office and we were essentially like, we need to change the website right away. And like, you know now, like, aesthetics are so important to us and all these things. At that moment, being clear in the messaging was the most important thing to us. We realized, I think there's not that many moments in your life when you realize, okay, this can be a defining moment, and everything can change based on what you do right now. There's not a lot of moments in people's lives like that. That was a clear moment in our life when we were like, if we make this decision and we lean into this, we don't know what the outcome will be, but we know that this is a once in a lifetime opportunity. So, we leaned all the way into it, and we put these big "banned by the NBA" in red letters across the website. And it went out. And seven minutes after it went out, our life changed. And so, when that happened, it was the number one news story in the world. Number two, three, and 17 most searched terms on Google. There were over a million articles written or posted about it within 10 days. We sold nine months of inventory in three days. And we just were like, I can't believe this is happening. And so, we leaned into it and we kept pushing. And it took us roughly four to five years to get to a strong inventory position where we had the ability to really start growing, expand into different categories. But just we could not keep up with the demand. And it was the best thing that ever happened to us. We had no money for marketing. And because of that, we're now able to sit here on stage with you today. Meena Flynn:      Let's fast forward today. Can you talk us through your business now and what the composition looks like and really a little bit about luxury performance and why you guys decided that's the category that I'm going to define? Ryan Goldston:   Yeah. So, we really wanted to create this category of luxury performance. And we knew that we had to start in a micro niche where we had authenticity and credibility. So, basketball shoes that instantly make you jump higher was the foundation for what we created. And we felt like would really open up the opportunity to create this category. So, like Adam said, for four years, we just sold men's basketball shoes exclusively through our website. Then June 17th, 2014, we launched our men's and women's running shoes. Our first retailer for men was Saks Fifth Avenue. Right away, we had the two top selling SKUs there. Our first retailer for women was Net-A-Porter, which we launched with on January 1st, 2015. Within six days, we became the fastest selling new designer of all time, hit our season's target sell through. And what we did is we grew our wholesale distribution from there. And while we started direct to consumer to begin with, the reason why we went to wholesale and really looked to build it out is we wanted to create this category and we wanted to do it in an authentic way that we felt like could scale and do it in meaningful way where there was authenticity with these retailers. So, luxury had always been defined by these retailers and there had never been performance in their stores. So, we knew that we could enter in, we could own this category, we could be a first mover, and we could bring something very differentiated within the market. That's why also in 2016, we became the first members from an athletic brand inducted to the CFDA. So, it was the first time they're saying not only is this sport and performance, but it's also luxury and fashion. And that kind of ties into what the thesis of the brand was when we were creating and is that there's these two pillars. One is sport and performance, the other is luxury and fashion. And we want to be the bridge that connects the two. Or it's like a Venn diagram. You have one circle that's sport and performance, the other that's luxury and fashion. And we wanted to sit at the center. So, we really focused on creating this category, entering in an authentic way, and then having the product that really you could change your clothes throughout the day and keep your footwear the same. Meena Flynn:      Can you talk to us about how your travels and your real-life experiences really helped you create Zipline? And why do you think this personal story also resonates with your consumers? Adam Goldston:   So, I think brands are living, breathing things. And so, as you become larger, there's definitely an opportunity where you lose some of those personal aspects. I think the fact that we are a founder-led brand gives us a unique advantage, specifically in the spaces which we exist. So, the Zipline, perfect example, was inspired by a trip that Ryan and I took to Tokyo, where we walked 14.3 miles in one day to get these Japanese souffle pancakes. So, they're these soft, fluffy, just like wobbly type of pancakes. And when we sat down, it was honestly Ryan that really, really wanted these. We looked at them, and Ryan was like, we need to create a compound that feels the way that these look. And so, we didn't walk there for inspiration. We walked there because we wanted pancakes. It turned into inspiring our number one selling shoe. But you never know when that inspiration is going to strike. And then the upper of the shoe was inspired by a trip that Ryan and I took to Dubai. So, we're speaking at this really large conference. And then we ended up going ziplining the next day. So, we went over the marina. And it feels like this incredibly freeing experience, but you can still move your limbs. So, you feel like you have this freedom, but that you're locked in. And so, when we were at home, it was during the pandemic, Ryan had put together a design brief for like how should we dream up of ideas. And we were reflecting on the things that were important to us, and like the trips that we had the most fun on and what we missed. And one of the experiences we had brought up was ziplining across the marina in Dubai. And Ryan said, what if we create an upper that feels the way that that experience felt and gives your foot the structural support that you need, but it also feels free. So, end up creating the Zipline off of that. And launched it in April of 2022. And it just continued to be incredible for us. It's a juggernaut for the business today. And for us, we've just tried to find inspiration in all aspects of our lives. Like, I think from where we started to where we're at today, we've been very lucky that we've got to do incredible things from our Formula One partnerships, travel across the world, create products that exist all across the world, build physical flagships. But all of those moments of inspiration have not been planned. It's simply from experiencing things. And I think, again, being a founder-led business, and we see it across plenty of businesses, it's a unique advantage because you're able to draw things from your mind and then bring them into the world at a faster rate than larger conglomerates could. And for us, we are always excited when we get struck with inspiration. And that was a combination of the two. And led to our best-selling product today. Meena Flynn:      I love that story. So, you talked about being founder led. You're also 100% founder owned. So, can you tell us why you have stayed fully independent? And also, this has been 17 years. You've had to scale and really be disciplined and also decide when to lean in. So, what has led that to be the right structure to date? Ryan Goldston:   I mean, it's a great question, because obviously, it's uncommon both from where we were and where the landscape has been. And a big part of that was we wanted to build the dynastic brand. And to do that, it takes making non-consensus right decisions where you're focused on the long-term. That being said, when we were initially starting, not only the professors, but most people that we talked to didn't believe in the idea and the concept. So, the fact was, we had this idea that was very unique, that was very different. We were entering into a very competitive landscape with a lot of apparent risk. But in our mind, the apparent risk actually lowered the competitive risk, because you're able to really stand for something different and be unique. And we've done it for 17 years. We believed in building a super, super strong foundation during that process because we felt like the most enduring brands spend the time on the front end, investing and showing who they are to the customer, to the market, and doing different things. I mean, when you just asked the question about the Zipline and how our personal story connected to the design of the product. And I think that's a big part of being founder led and founder owned is that we're able to invest in these different moments that we believe in, that we feel strongly about, that traditionally wouldn't be something that would connect with an investor if you're describing it. But once it's built, there's a real connection to it. Whether it's talking about Japanese souffle pancakes with a performance sneaker, or even the flagships that we've designed. When creating the luxury performance category, we've looked at it from a very different lens. And it's been our belief that investing in areas that are unique to us, that create this competitive moat, that are able to own this category, so we're able to be very different from what else exists in the market, has been something that we're passionate about, that has taken time to build, but has allowed us to do something very different. And so, I would say that being 17 years in, having never raised any outside capital, and being able to build APL and a brand that is super unique, has allowed us to create this category where even though we're 17 years in, we still feel like we're at the very beginning, and there's all this runway in front of us, because of this dynastic lens that we've looked at the business and the brand through. And also, just the sheer opportunity that's in front of us. And I think that realizing that there's people that now really believe in it. And knowing that there's a belief in the category, in the brand, the enduring aspect of APL, and the fact that we have something very, very special within the market. Adam Goldston:   So, I think one of the other things about Ryan and I too, as leaders and CEOs, but also as founders, is that you have to be flexible in terms of the path that you want to take. So, like, you want to be very strict in terms of, like, how you make specific decisions and whatnot, but you need to be flexible in the path because none of us have a crystal ball. And so, we've made a lot of, to Ryan's point, non-consensus right decisions to get to where we're at today. And the luxury of being 100% independent allowed us to do that. But as we think of becoming the definitive world leader of luxury performance, we always have to have our mind open. And so, I think that that tight stubbornness in the beginning has also got us to the point that we're at today. But like, as we continue to grow, so did our aperture of the world. So, I think that now we have a more open idea in terms of how do we grow the business. Meena Flynn:      Let's go to a quote that I think you shared with me, which is a Larry Ellison quote that stuck with you, which is the bigger the apparent risk, the fewer people will try to go there. How do you compete in a category that has so much scale already embedded in it? And what does it take really to stay differentiated and really not lose your unique brand, your identity, your values? Ryan Goldston:   So, that's a quote that Adam has referenced from the beginning of the company. And it's something that's guided us in a lot of ways. I mean, I said it earlier, but it is true. The greater the apparent risk, potentially the lower the competitive risk, because there are less people that are going to go into the market. Even though there's a lot of big competition, there are less people. The way that we always defined it was it's this massive ocean, and we can be a paradise or utopia within it, which allows us to be true to ourselves, different from whatever exists within the market. And you're able to have this North Star that guides you through. The other part of that is by going and creating something different and unique, and like I said, this bridge that connects sport and performance and luxury and fashion, you have a very large TAM. And that's just a real thing where you're getting to play in both markets, be different in both. So, in sport and performance, we sit at the top when it comes to price, design, material. Our design philosophy, when you think about it compared to what else exists within the market is we don't use big and blazing logos. We let the material, the color, the technology, and design tell the story. And that's very luxury coded in the process of what we create. And then within the luxury space, the fact that we have these underpinnings in our foundation is in performance and shoes that instantly make you jump higher, instantly make you run faster, allows us to really stand out within the market and offer something completely different. And so, for us, we're able to look at it from that perspective. And it allows us to really be differentiated in two very large markets, be true to ourselves. And I think a lot of times when you're creating a business, choosing the correct market and the correct positioning for your brand defines what your opportunity is not only now, but into the future. And we picked two large markets with a unique positioning in both. And while there weren't very many competitors, it allowed us to be something that is really, really special. And as the years go on, we get more confidence in that decision and the uniqueness of the spot that we sit at. Meena Flynn:      Well, I would say it's just so inspiring to hear the background of, you know, back at USC to where you are now, the relationship that you have with each other, and really where you're going to be able to take this business. And like you said, you're still in the early innings and we got a lot of runway. But we're just really grateful for the two of you guys joining us today. So, thank you.
